The NATO alphabet is also called the ICAO radiotelephony spelling alphabet.
ICAO spells the letter A as alfa, with one L.
ICAO spells the letter J as juliett, with two T's.
The letter X is spoken as x-ray, which is why some old charts print it with a hyphen.
Pilots describe a clear radio signal as five by five.
Roger means a message has been received. Wilco means the instruction will be carried out.
Over means the speaker is finished and expects a reply. Out means no reply is expected.
Mayday is the distress call. Pan-pan is used for an urgent situation that is not yet life threatening.
A squawk code is a four-digit number assigned to an aircraft by air traffic control.
SOS was chosen because its Morse pattern is simple to send and recognise. It does not stand for save our souls.
Radio operators repeat numbers one digit at a time to avoid mistakes. Nine becomes niner and five becomes fife.
A callsign identifies a station or aircraft on a radio frequency.
Readability and signal strength are often reported on a scale of one to five.
Say again is the standard request to repeat a transmission.
